# Week 2 build write-up
Built a web-search agent with two tools. Latency was the main issue.

Evaluating agents
pass@k vs pass^k
Proxy vs direct measures

# Evaluating agents

## pass@k vs pass^k
pass@k: any of k runs succeeds. pass^k: all k succeed. Reliability is what deployment needs.

## Proxy vs direct measures
A quiz score is a proxy. Retention a week later is closer to the thing itself.

# Evaluating agents

## pass@k vs pass^k
pass@k: any of k runs succeeds. pass^k: all k succeed. Reliability is what deployment needs.

## Proxy vs direct measures
A quiz score is a proxy. Retention a week later is closer to the thing itself.

# Agent environments

## What an environment is
State, observations, actions, dynamics. The reward is a separate claim about what matters.

## Partial observability (POMDP)
When the agent cannot see the full state it must maintain a belief and sometimes act to gather information. Measurement can be an action with a cost.

## Attention as a hidden variable
Learners do not read everything shown to them. Attention gates learning and drains with fatigue.

args.text:
Yes — here is the core idea as plainly as possible:

pass^k means the agent must succeed on every one of k runs.
- if all k runs succeed, pass^k = 1
- if even one run fails, pass^k = 0

Example with 3 seeds:
- successes on 3/3 seeds -> pass^3 = 1
- successes on 2/3 seeds -> pass^3 = 0

So pass^k is stricter than pass@k and is used to measure reliability.

For your writeup, you can say:
'I report pass^k, where pass^k equals 1 only if the agent succeeds on all k runs, and 0 otherwise. This metric captures reliability across seeds.'

Now you do one tiny check: if your agent succeeds on seeds 1 and 2 but fails on seed 3, what is pass^3?
